analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate drug prices directly and lets Americans import cheaper prescription drugs from abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 2 cosponsors in February 2006, it was referred to three House committees and died there when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have scrapped the rule that bars the Health and Human Services Secretary from negotiating Medicare drug prices, and required the Secretary to bargain with drugmakers directly, the way the VA does, to get beneficiaries the lowest possible price. It also would have let pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals legally import qualifying prescription drugs from approved countries, banned drugmakers from punishing importers, and extended the 2006 Medicare drug-plan enrollment deadline while waiving late-enrollment penalties. It never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and other consumers paying U.S. prescription prices. Direct government negotiation, modeled on the VA's bulk purchasing, would replace the system in which prices are set only by private plans, and legal importation would give consumers access to the lower prices charged in other countries. The bill's findings claim Americans pay up to 10 times more than consumers elsewhere and estimate savings of at least $635 billion over a decade [S3]. Seniors who missed the 2006 enrollment deadline would also have been spared the late-enrollment penalty through the end of 2006 [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and other consumers buying prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'non-interference' provision that bars the HHS Secretary from influencing drug-price negotiations, and instead requires the Secretary to negotiate contracts with drug manufacturers, using authority similar to the VA and other federal bulk buyers, to ensure beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price [S2, S3].

Requires HHS, within 180 days, to write regulations allowing pharmacists, pharmacies, wholesalers, and individuals to import qualifying drugs from approved countries, with registered exporters, FDA inspections, laboratory testing, and counterfeit-resistant packaging requirements [S2, S3].

Makes it unlawful for manufacturers to punish importers by charging them higher prices, denying or delaying supplies, or changing formulations to block importation — enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission with triple damages and by state attorneys general suing on residents' behalf [S2, S3].

Removes the patent-infringement barrier to selling in the U.S. a patented drug first sold abroad by the patent owner, and extends the 2006 Medicare drug-plan enrollment period through November 14, 2006, with late-enrollment penalties suspended through December 2006 [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose U.S. prices would face direct government negotiation and competition from lower-priced imports, and who could no longer use price discrimination, supply cutoffs, reformulation, or patent suits to choke off importation [S2, S3]. Registered exporters would also pay an annual registration fee — $10,000 in the first year — capped at 1% of the value of drugs exported, to fund FDA inspections and enforcement [S3].

drawbacks.text: Importation shifts safety enforcement onto a new system of foreign exporters: the bill relies on FDA registration, unannounced inspections, laboratory testing by importers, and counterfeit-resistant packaging, but a badly run version of this channel could let unsafe or counterfeit drugs reach patients, and the bill's own findings concede that an unaffordable drug market was already pushing Americans toward unregulated sources [S3].

The dramatic savings figures in the bill — up to 1,000% price gaps and $635 billion in consumer savings — appear in the bill's own 'findings' section rather than an independent analysis, and lower prices from government negotiation or importation would come out of pharmaceutical revenue that funds research and development, the standard objection to both provisions [S3].

The bill touches patents, food and drug law, and Medicare law at once, which is why it was referred to three separate committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — a structure that makes passage harder and invites each committee to trim provisions outside its jurisdiction [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For beneficiaries the upside is concrete and large: Medicare drugs are a major household expense, and the negotiation provision simply gives the government the same bargaining power the VA already uses, while importation adds an escape valve to world prices [S2, S3]. The safety risks of importation are real but were addressed in the bill through registered exporters, fees to fund inspections, testing, and counterfeit-resistant packaging [S3]. The weaker part of the bill is its evidence: the headline savings numbers are the sponsors' own findings, not an independent estimate, so the actual savings from negotiation were uncertain [S3]. On balance a straightforward attempt to lower drug costs whose main design flaw was bundling too much into one bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2006 and sent to three House committees, then to a Health subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2007 without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Larsen introduced the bill on February 16, 2006, with Rep. Jim McDermott as the other original sponsor [S3, S5].
The bill had only 2 cosponsors, both Democrats [S4].

On introduction it was referred to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Judiciary — and the next day it was sent to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; no committee or subcommittee ever acted on it, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 with the bill still parked there [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the non-interference clause protecting their U.S. pricing stayed on the books, drug importation remained barred, and Medicare continued to buy through private plans rather than negotiating directly. Seniors continued paying the prices the private-plan system produced.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committees to which the bill was referred never acted on it.

industries.note: Direct government negotiation of Medicare prices, legal reimportation, an antitrust-style ban on punishing importers, and a patent carve-out for drugs first sold abroad would all cut into U.S. prices and revenue. Because the bill died, the non-interference clause that protects their pricing remained law [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and private drug plans
industries.note: The non-interference clause the bill would repeal is what keeps Medicare drug pricing in private hands: plans and their PBM middlemen negotiate with manufacturers instead of the government. Requiring the HHS Secretary to negotiate directly would have displaced part of that middleman role [S2].

The bill creates a legal importation channel: exporters register with the FDA (a $10,000 first-year fee, capped at 1% of export value), submit to unannounced inspections, and get listed publicly so consumers can verify them. Their gain is consumers' access to cheaper drugs [S3].
